entries.title: UK court hands comedian Russell Brand 10.5 years for rape, sexual assault
entries.summary: This is a breaking news story.
entries.content:
A British court has sentenced comedian and actor Russell Brand to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault.

London’s Southwark Crown Court handed down the sentence on Monday. Brand was convicted last week of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more between 2004 and 2009.

The British media personality, known for outrageous stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, asserted that he was innocent and all his encounters were consensual.

However, a jury of eight men and four women on Thursday convicted him for attacks on four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

His victims delivered powerful statements during the sentencing hearing, describing the trauma his attacks had caused.

More to come…

entries.title: Iran stands by demands to end the war as US ramps up military pressure
entries.summary: Talks aimed at preventing new major fighting between the US and Iran are ongoing.
entries.content:
Talks aimed at preventing new major fighting between the US and Iran are ongoing.

Tehran, Iran – The Iranian government has reported more strikes by the United States but insists this pressure will not impact its demands to end the war.

Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor for Hormozgan, where the overnight US strikes hit, confirmed on Monday morning that the southern island of Qeshm was targeted but no residential and commercial areas or vital infrastructure were damaged.

The US did not directly acknowledge the air strikes, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated Washington’s characterisation of similar recent strikes on Qeshm as “defensive”. Previous attacks, the latest of which was acknowledged by President Donald Trump on Friday, have targeted Iranian air defences and radar installations.

Mediators are trying to prevent large-scale US attacks on Iran, which Trump has repeatedly threatened, with talks continuing. But Washington appears unwilling to accept Iran’s seven demands to end the war, which include the lifting of the US blockade on Iran’s southern ports and lifting sanctions on Tehran.

Seven demands

Esmail Baghaei, the spokesman of Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on Monday rejected Rubio’s remarks that some of these seven demands were “ridiculous and really not realistic”.

“Iran’s plan is still the most logical plan on the table. I think it can lead to security returning to the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, and create the grounds for a process,” Baghaei said during a news conference in Tehran.

The terms mostly amount to a return to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed in June between Iran and the US. But Tehran now has additional stipulations regarding the future of the Strait of Hormuz.

Baghaei said the US announcement of a reward of up to $20m for information on Iran’s nuclear programme is a ploy by the Trump administration to “convey the sense that the Iranian nuclear issue is still a threat”, after the Republican Party’s heavy defeats in midterm elections.

Tehran says it will not part with its highly enriched uranium, which is believed to be buried under the rubble of facilities bombed by the US and Israel last year. But it is open to downblending the material, which would be needed to build a nuclear bomb.

International inspectors have no access to Iranian nuclear sites, except for the Bushehr nuclear power plant, where the Foreign Ministry said there was a recent visit.

Iran has accused the International Atomic Energy Agency and its director, Rafael Grossi, of stepping out of their technical mandate and creating the grounds for attacks on nuclear facilities during last year’s 12-day war and the current war.

There have been signs of a positive breakthrough in mediation efforts, with reports that Trump and Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani will meet in the White House on Monday.

But Andreas Krieg, an associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Washington’s biggest objection to the ongoing mediated talks is that Iran is essentially demanding the rewards of an agreement before providing the concessions to justify one.

“Reopening Hormuz within two days sounds accommodating, but it changes the timetable rather than the substance of the bargain,” he told Al Jazeera about the Iranian proposal.

Both the US and Iran’s Arab neighbours would not accept long-term Iranian-approved shipping corridors in the Strait of Hormuz.

Rubio and other officials are also against Iran’s demand for an end to hostilities across the region, as it would restrict Israel’s military freedom of action.

“Iran is going beyond a ceasefire, trying to translate its wartime leverage into a new regional security arrangement on its own terms,” Krieg said.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Sunday that the country’s military mission in Iran remained unfinished, and threatened Lebanon’s Hezbollah with further territorial losses if it joined an Iranian attack.

Tankers and navigation systems targeted

Iranian authorities continue to warn ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz to refrain from taking “unauthorised” routes or face potential attacks.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman Hossein Mohebbi rejected the claim by the US that all naval mines have been cleared from the Strait of Hormuz.

“Nobody dares enter the Strait of Hormuz to remove the mines,” he said on Sunday.

Iranian state television reported on Monday that 11 tankers have been attacked over the past 10 days, with four unable to continue transit.

IRGC-affiliated media cited an unnamed IRGC Navy source as claiming on Monday that maritime navigation systems were targeted in the southern areas of the waterway overnight, preventing tankers from transiting as part of the US-coordinated oil shuttle system.

Trump played down the prospects of a return to all-out war with Iran on Sunday, but added that the US military had marked civilian infrastructure like 38 bridges as targets if the war restarts at scale.

Krieg said he expects Tehran to continue its strategy of “controlled escalation” rather than immediate all-out retaliation against the US strikes.

“The new American effort to disrupt Iran’s overland trade will reinforce this strategy. Tehran will increasingly seek to make the Gulf states bear the economic consequences of Washington’s decisions, hoping they will pressure Trump towards compromise,” Krieg said.

“Washington may believe it is conducting a limited campaign of coercion, while Tehran increasingly sees an unrestricted economic war against its survival. At some point, Iran may decide that the costs of continued restraint exceed the risks of escalation.”

entries.title: More than 100,000 sign petition for inquiry into UK role in Gaza genocide
entries.summary: The number of signatures requires the British parliament to consider the topic for debate.
entries.content:
The number of signatures requires the British parliament to consider the topic for debate.

A petition calling for a public inquiry into Britain’s “complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza” has gathered more than 100,000 signatures.

The petition posted on the UK Parliament website reached the threshold on Monday, requiring parliament to consider the topic for debate.

The initiative demands “an inquiry into any British involvement in Israeli operations in Gaza,” including “the sale, supply or use of weapons, surveillance aircraft and Royal Air Force bases”.

The petition was launched by Jennifer Forbes, chair of the executive committee of Your Party, a left-wing party launched by former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn – who serves as its parliamentary leader – and other left-wing figures in the UK.

Signatories called for an inquiry that has the power to question government ministers and officials involved in decision-making around the UK’s role in the war, particularly regarding the supply of arms to Israel.

“We are not going away until we get this inquiry. We want the truth, and we want justice,” Jeremy Corbyn said in a post on X.

The UK is a longstanding ally of Israel and has reportedly supported the country’s genocidal war on Gaza.

A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera revealed that the UK provided military support to Israel by creating an air bridge that was vital to sustain the intensity of the war on Gaza. Furthermore, UK-based companies and factories supply crucial parts found in jets that are used to bomb Gaza.

However, experts say the UK’s policy towards supporting Israel has shifted in recent months. After assuming leadership in July, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the ruling Labour Party “got wrong” its position on Israel, and accepted that it caused “huge hurt”.

It is not unusual for parliamentary petitions to reach 100,000 signatures in the UK. Examples of petitions active right now with more than 100,000 signatures include one on reducing the pension age and another that demands a stop to the addition of folic acid to flour.

The petitions do not require lawmakers to do anything more than consider the topic for a debate.

entries.title: ‘No concession’: What to expect from Russia-US-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
entries.summary: A fourth round of peace talks in 2026 takes place this week, with security guarantees high on the agenda.
entries.content:
A fourth round of peace talks in 2026 takes place this week, with security guarantees high on the agenda.

Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are set to converge in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for negotiations aimed at ending nearly five years of war between Moscow and Kyiv.

But analysts are not hopeful of much progress in the trilateral talks slated for Tuesday and Wednesday amid US President Donald Trump’s recent engagement with the Kremlin.

Trump has blamed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for holding up peace efforts. “Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” he said last month. The US also signed a deal last month to buy Russian diesel, which critics say would provide Russia with revenue to sustain the war against Ukraine.

On Thursday, Trump claimed that the war was close to being settled, and ending it might involve all of Europe. But Europe is not officially part of the trilateral talks. Last week, France said that Europe will send representatives to Abu Dhabi, as Ukraine’s Western allies fear Trump might force a deal that might undermine the continent’s security.

Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war that has killed thousands and displaced millions.

So what can we expect from the latest round of peace talks this year, as tit-for-tat attacks on energy sites have intensified in recent months? The two sides have held three rounds of US-mediated peace talks this year, including two in Abu Dhabi.

Who is attending the talks?

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will be heading the US delegation for the first such talks in nine months, as the US president has pushed to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.

Ukraine’s primary negotiator and foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov will lead Kyiv’s negotiation team, the Kyiv Independent reported. The Ukrainian delegation will also include David Arakhamia, head of Zelenskyy’s parliamentary group; Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov; and Sergiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the Presidential Office.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, confirmed last week that the Russian delegation would be led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported. It also includes diplomat Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yuri Zhygarlovsky, the Kremlin said.

On Monday, the Kremlin said the peace talks would not include European officials. Peskov’s comments to reporters appeared to conflict with a statement on Sunday by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who said officials from France, Britain, Germany, NATO and the European Commission would be present at the November 10-11 meeting.

An EU official told the AFP news agency on Monday that national security officials for the bloc, NATO, France, Germany and the United Kingdom would be on site – but it was unclear how they would be involved.

What is at stake in the Abu Dhabi talks?

“I don’t expect any tangible progress in the Abu Dhabi talks. The reason is simple and remains the same – Putin has absolutely no intention to negotiate seriously. He remains totally fixated on the [destruction] of Ukraine,” Oleksandr Merezhko, a Ukrainian member of parliament from the Servant of the People party, told Al Jazeera.

Putin wants Ukraine’s “surrender”, which will allow him to subjugate Ukrainians, he said.

Finnish-Russian political scientist Arkady Moshes says Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence are at stake in the upcoming talks.

Restoring Ukrainian territorial integrity, including Crimea, may already be beyond reach, said Moshes, a programme director at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. Russia annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014 – a move not recognised by the United Nations.

Moshes said that it would be very difficult for Ukraine to accept a peace agreement that doesn’t allow it “to choose its alliances, decide on its security future, or [that] put limits on its military”.

Ukraine wants Russia to withdraw from its territory and a security guarantee as part of any deal with Russia, but Russia has refused to end its occupation and set conditions that Kyiv should not be given membership of the NATO alliance. Moscow has also opposed the deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine after a deal.

Matthew Boyse, a senior fellow with Hudson Institute’s Center on Europe and Eurasia specialising in Central Europe, agreed that the most difficult sticking points are those about territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.

“So far Putin has not budged from his ‘my way or the highway’ and ‘what’s mine is mine and what’s yours is negotiable’ position,” Boyse, a former US diplomat, told Al Jazeera.

The analysts agreed that the future of European security as a whole is also at stake.

“The Kremlin agreed to and codified the post-1991 European security order in many agreements and treaties until Putin in the 2000s began to tear them up and in 2014 turned that order upside down,” said Boyse, referring to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

But the Kremlin has accused the US and its European allies of encircling Russia militarily. To that end, Russia has opposed the expansion of NATO in Europe, which it sees as a security threat. Russia has warned of a direct military standoff with Europe if NATO expands its military footprint eastward closer to the Russian border.

Anders Olofsgard, deputy director at the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics, said it was reassuring that Kushner had explicitly stated that “NATO would remain central to European collective defence and that no country should have a veto over another country’s security or alliance choices”.

Another element at stake is the future of post-Soviet states in Europe, namely Belarus, Moldova, Georgia and Armenia, said Moshes, the political scientist.

“If Ukraine now capitulates despite its serious efforts and despite the support from the West, from Europe, that means that several other post-Soviet states will definitely be under threat,” he said, adding that Russia could pursue a “tough Soviet-like sphere of influence or even direct annexation” of these countries.

When was the last time a breakthrough appeared likely?

No talks have yet come close to a breakthrough.

Only perhaps at the end of March 2022, at the very start of the conflict, when the two countries met in Istanbul, there was some possibility of ending the conflict, said Olofsgard.

“At this point, the relative strengths of the two counterparts were not clear; Ukraine had proven stronger and Russia more incompetent than expected,” he said.

Ukraine was also more willing to make concessions with respect to joining NATO, not allowing foreign bases in Ukraine, and not demanding the immediate return of Crimea, Olofsgard added.

Ultimately, however, there were many factors contributing to the meeting’s failure in the end, “including the atrocities in Bucha, [a] lack of clear Western promises of security guarantees, Russian failures on the battlefield changing the calculations of both sides, and incompatible views on land concessions and military build-up of Ukraine”, he said.

Analysts talk about a guarantor to secure peace. They point out the example of American troops stationed in South Korea to this day following the 1953 Korean War armistice.

Ukraine would “probably need something like that”, Moshes said, adding that “no Western country has been seriously speaking about guaranteeing whatever the outcome of the negotiations might be”.

Why have repeated attempts to negotiate an end to this war failed?

Vast differences remain between the two sides.

While past meetings have facilitated important results, from prisoner exchanges to the return of kidnapped Ukrainian children from Russia, they have failed to address core differences, said Boyse, referring to territorial concessions and a security guarantee for Ukraine.

Ultimately, Russia wants to win the war – it wants a military victory over a diplomatic one, said Moshes.

“Russia is interested in continuing the war until Ukraine is defeated,” he said, adding that “Ukraine cannot accept capitulation after so many years of resistance [and] so much economic trouble”.

Boyse, the former US diplomat, said that Putin’s grand vision of reestablishing the Russian empire was the key obstacle.

“Putin has a colonial attitude towards Ukraine. He wants to control it or at a minimum, decide what goes on there,” said Boyse, adding that this was understandably unacceptable to Ukraine.

What would it take for these talks to produce a meaningful breakthrough?

Olexiy Haran, a Ukrainian professor of comparative politics at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, said some technical issues could be negotiated in Abu Dhabi this week, including grain supplies, a ceasefire in the Black Sea, an energy ceasefire and perhaps another exchange of prisoners.

But all the analysts were certain no peace accord would emerge from the talks.

“The White House has hinted at what appears to be some sort of a grand bargain that appears to expand the number of issues under negotiation to the European security order,” said Boyse.

But this assurance appears to focus primarily on meeting Russia’s demands, not Ukraine’s, he said.

“Russia is the demandeur and the aggressor and is pressing a weakened president who very much wants to be a peacemaker,” said the former US diplomat.

“Putin thinks he can win at the negotiation table what he cannot win on the battlefield.”

Olofsgard of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics said that Trump, who has become a lame-duck following his party’s losses in the midterm elections, may pay more attention to foreign policy during his remaining two years in power.

“This could imply that Trump will push even harder to make peace, or at least a ceasefire, in Ukraine. And given his past tendencies, that means leaning on Ukraine to make more concessions and trying to strike some kind of US business deals as a sweetener for Russia,” he said.

Analysts doubt a breakthrough would be achieved in the Abu Dhabi talks as the Russian leader would not offer major concessions.

“Putin’s way of negotiating is generally: demand the maximum, escalate, and wait until others compromise,” said Boyse.

entries.title: What ‘catastrophic’ South Africa local election results mean for ANC
entries.summary: The country is transitioning away from the era of ANC electoral dominance towards a more fragmented political system.
entries.content:
The country is transitioning away from the era of ANC electoral dominance towards a more competitive and fragmented multiparty political system.

South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) has recorded its worst-ever result in local elections, more than three decades after the party of Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democratic rule.

While the ANC remains the country’s largest party, Wednesday’s vote appeared to confirm it is locked in a downward spiral amid long-held anger over corruption scandals and poor service delivery.

The elections were held to choose local government councillors who run South Africa’s eight biggest cities as well as its 44 district and 205 local municipalities. ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula described the results of the vote as “catastrophic”.

President Cyril Ramaphosa, who also serves as the president of the ANC, said political parties should approach upcoming political negotiations to form coalitions for local rule with humility. “Our people’s interest must not be drowned by the ⁠quest of political parties or representatives to settle political scores or petty squabbles,” he said.

What are the results of the vote?

The ANC won 31 percent of the vote, versus about 25 percent for its main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA).

The DA has sought to shed its historical reputation as a “white party”, a label it rejects. The party said it had won the votes of more than one million Black South ⁠Africans for the first time, based on its modelling.

The ANC lost its place as the largest party to the DA in the economic hub of Johannesburg, the capital Pretoria, and the large Ekurhuleni municipality east of Johannesburg. The DA also retained its control of South Africa’s second-biggest city, Cape Town.

While the ANC remained the largest party in terms of vote share, the results represent a sharp drop from the 46 percent it bagged in the 2021 local vote and less than half the vote share that the party had two decades ago: 66 percent in 2006.

In 2024, it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in a national election, which brought about a coalition national government and a seismic shift in South African politics with the end of the ANC’s 30-year dominance.

South Africa held its first democratic elections in 1994, when the ANC won 63 percent of the vote under Mandela’s leadership. He was inaugurated as the first Black president of South Africa shortly afterwards.

Sandile Mnguni, a lecturer in political science and international relations at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, said the “decline in electoral support should serve as a clear warning that the party can no longer rely on its historical political dominance or liberation credentials to retain the confidence of voters”.

“If the underlying grievances of the electorate remain unaddressed, the party could face even greater electoral challenges,” he told Al Jazeera.

What does this vote mean for the ANC?

Since no party won more than 50 percent of the vote in many cities, the ANC and DA have to team up or hash it out with smaller parties to form municipal governments. Parties have 14 days to negotiate before city councils are formed.

An ANC partnership with the DA would mirror an arrangement they have had in national government for the past two years, but the two are ideologically opposed on key issues ⁠such as how to address the deep economic and social inequalities left by apartheid.

The DA will be mindful of striking a partnership with the ANC, which analysts say was harshly rebuked by voters in this election over problems with basic services such as irregular water, electricity outages, dilapidated roads, broken street lights, and uncollected refuse.

Ramaphosa was also punished for being implicated in a corruption scandal known as “Farmgate” after burglars broke into his luxury private ranch in 2020 and stole $580,000 hidden inside furniture. The president was accused of covering up the theft and keeping efforts to trace the burglars private in a bid to avoid an investigation into where the money had come from.

South African author and political commentator Ralph Mathekga told Al Jazeera that the vote sent a “strong message” to the ANC “that the collapse of service delivery and the ensuing corruption has reached a point where it cannot be tolerated”.

Mathekga said voters no longer see the party as the solution to the problems faced by South Africans, but as the “chief culprit”.

“The elections were clearly a referendum on the ANC ‘s capacity to govern and turn the corner,” he noted.

South African political analyst and columnist Sipho Seepe said the vote was also a personal rebuke of Ramaphosa, who sought to present himself as a politically savvy and business-oriented leader for the party, but who has continually been accused of underperforming.

“He has been a total disaster, and the people this time have made it very clear,” Seepe told Al Jazeera. “People have been giving it [the ANC] a chance, and [now] they’re saying no more.”

The DA suggested it would steer clear of an agreement with the ANC when it said in a statement that it would initiate coalition discussions with “political parties that share a commitment to clean and accountable government, rooting out corruption, service delivery for all, the rule of law, and non-racialism”.

Ramaphosa is expected to step aside as party leader ahead of the 2027 ANC leadership contest and the country’s next general election in 2029.

What does this vote mean for South Africa?

The local election has ramifications for South Africa’s politics beyond local government.

Analysts say the vote confirms that the country is transitioning away from one-party dominance and towards political plurality. “From now on, we can accept coalitions to be the new normal,” Seepe said.

While this might lead to some political instability, the analyst said it may pressure parties to prioritise performance once in power. “The ANC government has been stable, but it has been failing the people,” he said, noting that being responsive to the electorate’s needs is now seen as more urgent than political continuity.

Mathekga, author of the book The ANC’s Last Decade, said voters have made it clear that they “do not want concentration of power in one party”.

“Coalitions are there to stay, perhaps until political parties demonstrate that they can be trusted with power to constitute government on their own,” Mathekga said, describing the shift as a “necessary evolution of South African politics”.

Mnguni, at the University of KwaZulu-Natal, agreed that South Africa appeared to be ready to trade a little less political stability in exchange for greater accountability.

“Of course, there may be instances of political stalemating, unstable alliances and disagreements that delay important municipal decisions [and] these risks should not be underestimated,” he said.

“However, I view the broader transition as an opportunity for South Africa’s democratic development, provided that political parties demonstrate political maturity and place governance above narrow partisan interests.”

entries.title: British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali defeats Mikiah Kreps for first ⁠⁠⁠⁠world title
entries.summary: Ali wins a controversial split-decision fight against American Kreps to claim IBO and WBF junior featherweight belts.
entries.content:
Ali, who fled Somalia’s civil war and settled in London, won the controversial split-decision fight against American Kreps to claim IBO and WBF junior featherweight belts.

Ramla Ali, a British Somali boxer whose life story is the subject of a new film, has realised a long-held dream and won her first world title to claim two vacant junior featherweight belts in the United States.

The 36-year-old landed the biggest titles of her career by winning the IBO and WBF belts in a controversial split-decision victory over American fighter Mikiah Kreps in Arlington, Texas, on Sunday.

The nail-biting nature of the 10-round contest should not have come as too much of a surprise, as the duo are former sparring partners and ended the night with an expression of mutual respect.

“Mikiah, I want to share this victory with you because you pushed me for 10 rounds,” an emotional Ali said while addressing her opponent, who she stopped from exiting the ring after being declared the winner.

“I kept saying I’m so tired because your work rate was next level. I don’t know how I kept up, so thank you for being such a great boxer.”

The 30-year-old Niagara Falls native reciprocated the emotion. “I respect you,” Kreps said as both fighters wrapped an arm around each other.

During the fight, Ali had Kreps on the canvas in round three, but she was behind her younger opponent in the overall punch count at the end of the fight.

The outcome of the fight caused controversy from the moment the referee lifted Ali’s arm when the decision was announced.

According to the official punch statistics from the fight, Kreps outlanded Ali by 115 blows to 78 and the American was also way ahead in the power shot count.

One judge scored the bout 98-91 for Kreps but the other judges saw the fight differently and gave Ali the win with scores of 97-92 and 96-93.

Veteran promoter Lou Di Bella wrote on social media, “Mikiah Kreps won that fight and it wasn’t even close. Stevie Wonder could see that.”

From Somalia’s civil war to world champion

The external noise would have mattered little to Ali, who dropped to her knees when the scores were announced.

Ali and her family are no strangers to adversity, having settled in London in 1992 after fleeing Somalia during its civil war.

Years after picking up the sport as a teenager in East London, Ali became the first Somali boxer to compete at the Olympic Games when she represented the country of her birth at Tokyo 2020. She later became the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title.

Ali’s journey has provided the inspiration for the movie ‘In the Shadows’ starring Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson.

The fighter lost her father earlier this year and said she stayed up all night prior to the fight, wishing he would have been around to see her in the ring.

“My father passed away in May, so I was really emotional,” she said in a post-fight interview with All The Smoke Boxing.

“Every round, I kept going to my corner to tell my coach I couldn’t do it any more because I was physically exhausted. I boxed through my skin and I’m glad I got the victory.”

Ali’s career has always been multi-dimensional. As a model and UNICEF ambassador, she has projected her voice beyond sporting arenas.

“I can’t put into words what this means to me and what this means to all of Somalia,” she said, fighting back tears, while standing inside the ring.

“I’ve hopefully inspired so many young girls and boys out there to dream big and that’s all I’ve ever wanted to do.”

entries.title: Paraguay raids ex-president’s home: Why a bank crash brought down Pena
entries.summary: Santiago Pena faces charges of financial crimes following Ueno Bank's collapse, impacting half of Paraguay's population.
entries.content:
Santiago Pena faces charges of financial crimes following Ueno Bank’s collapse, which impacted half of Paraguay’s population.

Paraguayan police have raided the home of ousted President Santiago Pena as part of an investigation into the collapse of one of the country’s largest digital banks.

The raid on Sunday comes after Ueno Bank’s downfall plunged the South American nation into its deepest economic and political crisis in recent years, sparking widespread protests.

Pena, an ally of US President Donald Trump who came to power in 2023, was removed from office on Friday after the collapse of Ueno froze access to the savings of nearly three million customers, almost half the country’s population of 6.5 million.

The former president, who has denied wrongdoing, faces criminal charges over allegations that he used his political influence to channel public money into the lender despite having financial ties to its parent company.

So, what charges does Pena face, and what does the bank scandal mean for the country’s future?

What do we know about the arrest?

Pena was arrested after Paraguay’s Senate voted unanimously on Friday to remove him from office, rejecting his attempt to resign a day earlier.

On Saturday, Judge Humberto Otazu ordered the former president to remain in pretrial detention at a military facility, saying the measure was necessary to ensure he remained in Paraguay while the investigation proceeded.

His lawyer, Ricardo Preda, said Pena would plead not guilty and would cooperate with investigators.

“What sets a serious country apart is not that its banks don’t fail, but how it responds,” Preda said on Friday. “If there is one thing that undermines confidence ⁠in the financial system, it is attempting to oust the president without evidence.”

Prosecutors also confirmed that police had searched Pena’s mansion outside the capital, Asuncion, as part of their investigation into the banking scandal.

Vice President Pedro Alliana has since been sworn in to replace Pena and is expected to serve out the remainder of his term until August 2028.

What has Pena been accused of?

Pena has been charged by prosecutors with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, offences that could each carry a prison sentence of up to 10 years.

The allegations are around Pena’s relationship with Ueno Bank, a digital lender launched in 2021 that rapidly expanded by offering banking services to Paraguayans who had previously been underserved by traditional financial institutions.

Pena held shares in Ueno’s parent company until March 2025. Prosecutors allege that while serving as president, he influenced government agencies and state-owned entities to deposit large sums of public money into the bank, despite concerns over its financial health.

By June, Ueno held approximately $850m in public funds, including money belonging to Paraguay’s state pension system.

Regulatory reports warning of excessive lending to certain companies had also emerged in recent months, raising questions about the bank’s solvency and its loans to businesses linked to its executives.

According to the indictment, Pena obtained two loans from Ueno worth approximately $500,000 in 2024 to construct his mansion. His monthly mortgage payment of $38,000 was reportedly six times his presidential salary.

The scandal has also implicated former Central Bank of Paraguay chief Carlos Carvallo, who previously headed Ueno. He has been charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, and has been ordered into pretrial detention.

Pena has rejected the allegations, maintaining that the bank’s difficulties were a regulatory matter.

Newly sworn-in President Alliana said on Sunday that the government had refunded 1.2 million Ueno Bank customers whose funds were frozen following the bank’s collapse.

He said approximately $158m had been paid out so far, with further reimbursements expected this week.

But analyst Andrew Nickson says Paraguay’s deeply politicised judicial system makes meaningful accountability unlikely following Pena’s arrest.

“The judicial system is so corrupt and politicised in favour of the [ruling] Colorado Party that only scapegoats are likely to suffer long-term sentences,” Nickson, a Paraguay expert at the University of Birmingham, told Al Jazeera.

The Colorado Party has held the presidency in Paraguay since 1948, except for five years between 2008 and 2013.

Nickson said he expects directors and senior officials at Banco Ueno and the Central Bank to face formal proceedings over the scandal but doubts that powerful political figures will face lasting consequences.

He said there had been two previous attempts since the 1990s to prosecute former Paraguayan presidents for corruption, both of which ended with charges being dropped on appeal.

“The same thing is likely to happen with Peña,” he said.

How has the scandal affected the country?

The collapse of Ueno Bank has left millions of Paraguayans struggling to access their savings, wages and pension payments, while raising questions about the government’s handling of public money.

The central bank intervened on Tuesday after discovering that Ueno had breached minimum solvency requirements.

The bank had made $146m in questionable loans to companies linked to its owner, while its corrected financial accounts showed its capital had fallen below half the legal minimum.

The crisis has sparked widespread protests, with thousands demanding access to their money and accountability from political leaders.

Some demonstrations have turned violent, with protesters clashing with police.

“We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history,” opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola said on Friday.

However, Nickson of the University of Birmingham said the country’s political and economic establishment is unlikely to face major upheaval following the crisis.

“The extraordinary control of the Colorado Party, the longest in power in the Americas, will remain intact,” Nickson said.

He said Paraguay’s economy, heavily dependent on soybean and meat exports, remains resilient, with agricultural exporters benefiting from the sharp depreciation of the local currency.

“In the longer term, the crisis will contribute to raising the consciousness of ordinary Paraguayans at the deep injustices in the country but ‘meaningful political reform’ will not be on the agenda of Alliana or the Colorado Party,” he added.

entries.title: Syria confirms sending troops to Saudi Arabia amid battle against Houthis
entries.summary: Syrian officials deny reports Damascus is sending troops to Yemen, but Syrian security integration appears under way
entries.content:
Syrian officials deny reports Damascus is sending troops to Yemen, but Syrian security integration appears under way.

Shortly after Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh last week, reports emerged that Damascus was aiding Saudi Arabia in its war against Yemen’s Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) and backed by Iran.

Security and financial aid appeared to be the cornerstone of the meeting between al-Sharaa and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which concluded with Riyadh pledging $403m in loans to help Syria rebuild infrastructure damaged by 13 years of its civil war.

Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates noted that cooperation between the two countries’ defence ministries was the “most notable” of the deals, but it did not elaborate.

Days after the visit concluded, media reports suggested Syria was sending fighters to Saudi Arabia to help fight the Houthis. The Reuters news agency reported that Syria was providing Riyadh with military advice and training inside the kingdom after Saudi cities were targeted in hundreds of Houthi missile attacks.

On Sunday, Syrian officials told The Associated Press news agency that Damascus has already sent Syrian military advisers to Saudi Arabia and 600 special forces were due to arrive in the kingdom next week.

Despite denying the initial reports, a Syrian government official told the state’s news agency SANA that Syrian soldiers were sent to Saudi Arabia in a “training, expertise exchange and military consultations” capacity.

“The Syrian role would probably count for more in Riyadh than on Yemen’s front lines because it would show that the new Syria can share a partner’s security burden,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian analyst, told Al Jazeera, adding that even a training and support role from the Syrian government rather than a direct combat role would satisfy Riyadh.

“The reports and the denials can both be partly right since Syrian officers training Yemeni forces inside the kingdom is different from Syrian troops fighting in Yemen. If Syrian forces are involved, Damascus has good reasons to avoid acknowledging it, from avoiding retaliation to reassuring Syrians that rebuilding at home comes first,” Hawach explained.

Houthi threat

Yemen has been a central concern for Saudi Arabia since Houthi fighters captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. Saudi Arabia has led an Arab military coalition to support Yemen’s internationally recognised government since March 2015. It has provided material and air support to anti-Houthi forces.

Saudi Arabia has been eager to form a regional military alliance that would help counter the threats from the Houthis and their patron Iran.

Tehran’s attacks on its Gulf neighbours since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28 and recent Houthi missile strikes on Saudi cities have highlighted the need for a regional security umbrella.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, agreed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, has been viewed as a mechanism for this collective defence by many in Riyadh.

Syria and its thousands of battle-hardened soldiers with some expertise in drone warfare would be considered a useful addition to this alliance. The Syrian official who spoke to SANA said the current military arrangement between Damascus and Riyadh could lead to Syria joining the Mecca Defence Alliance.

“Interest in the Mecca pact could reflect Syria’s wish to anchor its recovery in a regional security framework. Yemen is far enough away for Damascus to present any role as standing by an Arab partner while Lebanon is next door, and intervention would reopen its history there and risk destabilising Syria itself,” Hawach said.

“However, distance does not make it cost-free. Confronting Iran’s allies anywhere invites retaliation, and soldiers killed far from home would be hard to justify to a public that expects peace to bring recovery.”

Syrian expertise

Syria’s post-war government has already come under pressure to act militarily outside its borders. US President Donald Trump has spoken numerous times this year about trying to get Syria to intervene in Lebanon to help disarm Hezbollah, another Iran-backed group.

Syrian rebels have been deployed to other conflicts in the Middle East and North Africa during their attempts to overthrow Bashar al-Assad’s government from 2011 to 2024. Syrian fighters allegedly took part in Azerbaijan’s war against Armenia in 2020.

“Syrians are combat-experienced and -capable, and they’re cohesive, so there’s a potential tactical advantage there,” Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer on security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

“Overall, this is very much a common Saudi approach to strategy and security issues, basically leaning on partners they courted through diplomatic links.”

Since the fall of al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Saudi Arabia is believed to have been instrumental in helping the US remove Assad-era sanctions on Syria, which has been critical in legitimising the post-war government in Damascus.

With Saudi Arabia now fully embroiled in the Yemen war by backing its internationally recognised government and being targeted by regular Houthi air attacks, the deployment of Syrian troops would provide it with additional expertise and guidance on how to confront the Houthis.

The AFP news agency reported that Syrians in Yemen are now leading drone operations against the Houthis although the Syrian government has denied these claims.

Samy Akil, senior programme adviser with The Syria Report website, said Syria’s cooperation gives Riyadh another ally in the region and potential partner in the Mecca Defence Alliance.

“Syria has so far tried to navigate different competing regional interests across several regional capitals. It tried to not align itself with a specific camp, but I think as time goes on, it needs to kind of start settling on [a] hierarchy in terms of regional partners, and obviously, Saudi Arabia is one of the top contenders to do so,” he told Al Jazeera.

“It’s basically signalling that Syria is willing to support and help with the limited resources and capabilities it has, but it also inadvertently legitimises the Syrian government’s foreign policy approach of supporting regional countries and kind of showcase that it is not only a country that is asking for support, but it is also a country willing to provide support.”

With Israeli raids and attacks on southwestern Syria continuing, Damascus could also benefit from having a regional power such as Saudi Arabia as an ally.

“The fact is that Syria recognises that it has little policy options to deter a further entrenchment of Israeli forces into southern Syria in [the] hope that the potential of joining the [Mecca] agreement would act somewhat of a deterrence to, at the very least, stop further encroachment of Israeli troops in Quneitra and Daraa.”

entries.title: Which Republicans are running for minority leadership roles in US Congress?
entries.summary: Republicans in US House and Senate will hold elections on Tuesday to select leadership after losing their majorities.
entries.content:
Republicans in the US House and Senate will hold elections on Tuesday to select leadership after losing their congressional majorities.

The United States midterm elections have reshaped the balance of power in Washington, DC, breaking the Republican Party’s grip on Congress.

With Democrats set to take control of both legislative chambers in January, Republicans are preparing for a change in congressional leadership.

On Tuesday, Republicans in the House of Representatives and the Senate will hold elections to select the party’s leaders through the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

Several senior positions are at stake, including minority leader, minority whip and conference chair. But what do these jobs entail, and who is competing for them?

What are the key minority leadership positions?

Because the US has long had a two-party system – revolving around Democrats and Republicans – each side organises its own leadership in the chambers of Congress.

The aim is to present a united front on legislation and other congressional matters.

When the 120th Congress is sworn in this January, the Republican Party will be in the minority in both chambers.

Democrats will have majorities of at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate and at least 254 in the House, which has a total of 435 voting members.

To organise as the minority party, Republicans will need to choose leaders for both the House and Senate.

The minority leader in a given chamber is the most senior member of whichever party holds the fewest seats. The leader serves as the party’s chief spokesperson, coordinates its legislative strategy and negotiates with the majority party.

The minority whip is the second-ranking leadership position. The whip counts votes, communicates with lawmakers and works to keep members united behind the party’s positions.

Republicans also elect other leadership positions, including the conference chair, who oversees internal party meetings and helps shape the party’s messaging. Committee chairs also need to be selected to help develop legislative priorities.

Who is running for House minority leadership?

The biggest contest in the House is for minority leader, with longtime rivals Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio competing for the position.

Scalise, who has held senior Republican leadership positions for more than a decade, served as House majority whip from 2014 to 2018 and minority whip from 2019 to 2022. He has put himself forward as an experienced leader who can unite the party and guide Republicans through their return to the minority.

Jordan, a founding member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus and a close Trump ally, is campaigning on a more aggressive approach to confronting the Democratic majority.

In a letter to colleagues, the Ohio lawmaker described himself as “battle-tested” and argued he could better coordinate the party’s response to Democrat-led investigations into the Trump administration.

The contest for minority whip, the party’s second-ranking position, is between current majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota and August Pfluger of Texas.

Emmer is seeking to retain the position. He has acknowledged the scale of the party’s midterm losses, but argued that Republicans must remain united as they move into the minority.

Pfluger, who chairs the Republican Study Committee, is making the case for a change in leadership. In a letter to colleagues, he said the party needed “fresh ideas” and a clearer strategy to win back the House in 2028.

Who will lead Senate Republicans?

Senate majority leader John Thune of South Dakota is seeking to retain his position as his party’s leader in the chamber.

That would make him the minority leader when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Thune, who succeeded longtime Republican Senate leader Mitch McConnell in 2025, has so far faced no public challenger for the seat.

Republican John Barrasso of Wyoming, currently the majority whip, is also expected to seek another term as the party’s second-ranking leader in the Senate.

There has been some pushback against holding the Senate leadership elections so soon after the midterm losses, though.

Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin has pushed to delay the vote, arguing Republicans should have more time to assess the election results.

“It’s not like we’ve got to quick-form a majority in the Senate and do all the things with the committees. We have time,” Johnson told Fox News.

“This is time for reflection. This is time not to just, quick, make a knee-jerk decision.”

Senators like Mike Lee of Utah have voiced support for Johnson’s campaign.

“We have no business holding Senate Republican leadership elections until: (1) we’ve had ample opportunity to discuss what happened on Tuesday, and (2) we know who’s going to be in our conference,” Lee wrote on social media.

What happens to Mike Johnson?

Mike Johnson will lose his position as House speaker when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. The speaker is elected by the entire House, and the majority traditionally nominates someone from within its party.

Johnson announced he will not seek the House minority leader position, clearing the way for Scalise and Jordan to compete for the top Republican post.

However, Johnson is not leaving Congress. He will remain a member of the House and continue representing his Louisiana district.

Tuesday’s internal party elections will determine who leads the Republicans through their transition to minority status as they prepare to challenge Democratic control of Congress.

The leadership race will also test whether Republicans intend to continue backing Trump’s agenda or rethink their approach.

entries.title: Sudan teachers go on strike over meagre salaries and dilapidated schools
entries.summary: Teachers across the country say their pay no longer covers basic living costs.
entries.content:
Teachers across the country say their pay no longer covers basic living costs.

Khartoum, Sudan – For 26 years, Amal Suleiman Ahmed al-Haj has worked as a secondary school teacher in Sudan.

But her monthly salary of 132,000 Sudanese pounds ($13.20) only covers her family’s basic needs for a few days. Just buying a cooking gas cylinder will set her back about 170,000 pounds ($17).

With teachers in Khartoum State no longer paid enough to survive, they have gone on strike for a third week.

“My salary does not cover even a quarter of our needs. It may not last a family more than three or four days,” Amal told Al Jazeera. “Teachers are extremely exhausted and have to find other jobs in the evenings to supplement their income. In reality, we have become secondary workers in the education sector.”

Underpaid and under pressure

Beyond their salary issues, teachers are also unhappy with the lack of opportunities for promotion and accumulated unpaid entitlements.

They are also worried about deteriorating conditions in schools, caused by war and a lack of investment. Some classrooms at Amal’s school are no longer suitable for teaching.

“There is a classroom where I teach and its roof has collapsed, leaving us directly exposed to the sun. This is the environment in which we teach, and it affects both us and the students,” Amal told Al Jazeera.

“Those of us who stayed in Sudan [during the war] lost out. We did not lose our jobs, but we were not working and were not receiving salaries. As a result, our outstanding payments accumulated with the government.”

Amal said that teachers have resorted to strike action after exhausting all official channels to demand their rights.

“We submitted memorandums to the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance and the presidential palace, but nothing came of it. We also spoke through the media, and there was no solution left except going on strike,” she said.

“How can a teacher educate students when they cannot afford to get to school, pay for transport or provide for their children?” she said.

Many teachers Amal knows are considering leaving the profession. Some have already quit their jobs, taken unpaid leave, or sought alternative sources of income.

Amal admits that the suspension of classes during the strike is negatively affecting her students. But with Sudan’s education system in crisis, she says teachers need at least the basic conditions necessary to do their jobs.

“Teachers are human beings. They have needs, families and responsibilities. How can they fulfil their educational mission under these pressures? Some teachers walk long distances to reach their schools, while others faint because of malnutrition and exhaustion,” she said.

“We are not asking for luxuries. We just want to be able to live, get to our schools and continue our educational mission.”

A long-haul strike

The Sudanese Teachers’ Committee has organised staggered, intermittent strikes to pressure the government into addressing teachers’ demands.

Sami al-Baqir, the committee’s spokesperson, said participation was initially widespread, but later declined after alleged attempts by the government to undermine the industrial action. The measures included relaxing administrative controls over staff attendance to make schools appear operational despite the strikes and providing model schools with mechanisms to generate additional funding. Some teachers also received partial outstanding payments from the government when new strikes were announced.

After a meeting between Sudanese ministers and unions last month, Prime Minister Kamil Idris ordered the payment of money owed to teachers across all Sudanese states. However, the government did not give a detailed payment schedule or address teachers’ other demands concerning salaries and allowances, leading to the continued impasse.

The Sudanese teachers’ union says it is braced for a long battle to resolve its members’ grievances.

“We called … [for] a long-haul strike to absorb the tactics the government is using. It tries to circumvent the problems rather than solve them,” al-Baqir told Al Jazeera.

Their demands include an increase in the minimum wage from 12,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.20) to 500,000 pounds ($50), based on poverty-line benchmarks and a cost-of-living study for a family of five conducted by the Sudanese Teachers’ Committee.

The body also wants three cabinet decisions made more than seven months ago to be implemented, including an increase in the meal allowance to 90,000 pounds ($9), the introduction of a housing allowance, and a 130,000-pound ($13) allowance to address salary disparities among public sector employees.

“These decisions were issued by the cabinet, but they have not been implemented so far. This indicates that the government is not serious about addressing teachers’ problems,” al-Baqir said.

Government responds

The ongoing war between the Sudanese army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which broke out in April 2023, has contributed to the problems faced by teachers and school administrators, al-Baqir explained.

“For schools to reopen, teachers to return and the education system to stabilise, the problems facing schools and teachers must be addressed,” he added.

The conflict has disrupted schooling, destroyed educational facilities and turned some into shelters for the displaced or military sites, depriving millions of children of access to education.

The UN has documented 67 attacks on schools in Sudan since 2024, alongside more than 150 reports of armed groups commandeering educational facilities.

Lily Neyestani-Hailu, head of education in emergencies at UNESCO, said the conflict had forced hundreds of thousands of children out of school and put millions more at risk of missing out on education.

She said about 30 percent of Sudan’s schools were damaged or closed due to the war and more than 1,400 schools had been attacked.

Other estimates say that nearly half of the country’s schools are not functioning because of war damage or because they are being used as shelters or military facilities.

According to Sudan Education Cluster data published in January, 97 percent of schools in North Darfur have stopped classes. Only 13 percent of schools are operational in South Darfur and just 27 percent in West Darfur – two of the areas that have been worst-hit by the war.

At least 8 million children are now out of school, according to the UN, with poverty-stricken parents sending their children to work to help cover rising living costs.

School closures, a lack of investment in education and underpaid teachers are putting huge pressure on Sudan’s public education system.

“We are genuinely afraid that public education will be phased out,” al-Baqir said. “The government’s disregard for teachers’ rights, its failure to spend on education and the current administrative disorder in schools all send a message to parents that anyone who can afford private education will take their children there.”
